title: Determinate structures-2
summary: Deflection is the subject here, and the four standard results (WL³/48EI, 5wL⁴/384EI, WL³/3EI, wL⁴/8EI) should be automatic. Note that deflection varies as L³ or L⁴, so span dominates everything — which is why serviceability, not strength, sizes many beams. The energy methods (Castigliano, unit load) are more general than Macaulay's method and are the ones to reach for with trusses. Influence lines and moving loads round out the subchapter and are where bridge questions come from.

sections.heading: The deflection equation and Macaulay's method
sections.body:
The **elastic curve** of a beam satisfies

> **EI d²y/dx² = M**

Integrating once gives the **slope** and twice the **deflection**, with two constants fixed by the boundary conditions:

| Support | Conditions |
|---|---|
| **Simply supported** | y = 0 at both ends |
| **Fixed** | y = 0 **and** dy/dx = 0 |
| Free end of a cantilever | Neither (both unknown) |
| Symmetry at mid-span | dy/dx = 0 |

**Macaulay's method** handles discontinuous loading with a single equation, using bracket terms that **vanish when negative**:

> **⟨x − a⟩ⁿ = (x − a)ⁿ when x > a, and 0 when x ≤ a**

So one expression covers the whole beam, and one pair of constants serves throughout. The rules in using it: write the moment expression for the **rightmost** section, include **every** load to the left, and **never expand a bracket that is negative**. A UDL that stops partway must be handled by **extending it to the end and cancelling it with an equal upward UDL** from that point — a device worth knowing because it converts an awkward case into a standard one.

**The four standard results** — these must be known outright:

| Beam and loading | Maximum deflection | At |
|---|---|---|
| **Simply supported, central point load W** | **WL³/(48EI)** | Mid-span |
| **Simply supported, UDL w** | **5wL⁴/(384EI)** | Mid-span |
| **Cantilever, point load W at free end** | **WL³/(3EI)** | Free end |
| **Cantilever, UDL w** | **wL⁴/(8EI)** | Free end |

And the slopes at the supports: **WL²/16EI** and **wL³/24EI** for the two simply supported cases.

**Two comparisons worth drawing.** A cantilever of length L deflects **16 times** more than a simply supported beam of the same span under a central point load (WL³/3EI against WL³/48EI) — which is why cantilevers are kept short. And a **fixed** beam under UDL deflects only **wL⁴/384EI**, one fifth of the simply supported value, showing again the value of continuity.

**The dominance of span.** Deflection varies as **L³ or L⁴**:

> Doubling the span multiplies deflection by **8** (point load) or **16** (UDL)

while the moment only multiplies by 2 or 4. That mismatch is why **serviceability, not strength, sizes many long-span beams** — the section needed to keep deflection acceptable is larger than the section needed to carry the moment.

**IS 456 deflection control** avoids the calculation altogether for ordinary cases by limiting the **span/effective depth ratio**:

| Beam | Basic span/depth |
|---|---|
| **Cantilever** | **7** |
| **Simply supported** | **20** |
| **Continuous** | **26** |

For spans over 10 m these are multiplied by **10/span**, and they are further modified by factors for the **tension** and **compression** steel percentages and for a **flanged** section. The final deflection including creep and shrinkage is limited to **span/250**, and the deflection occurring **after** partitions are built to **span/350 or 20 mm**, whichever is less — because that is the part that cracks finishes.

These are **deemed-to-satisfy** rules: meet them and no explicit deflection calculation is required. They also explain why a concrete beam's depth is usually decided at the very start of a design, from the span, before any load is considered.

sections.heading: Moment-area and conjugate beam methods
sections.body:
**Mohr's theorems (the moment-area method):**

> **Theorem I:** the **change in slope** between two points equals the **AREA** of the M/EI diagram between them.
> **Theorem II:** the **deflection** of one point from the tangent at another equals the **MOMENT of that area** about the first point.

These are most efficient where the **M/EI diagram is simple** and where there is a point of **known zero slope** to measure from — which makes them ideal for **cantilevers** (zero slope at the fixed end) and for **symmetrically loaded simply supported beams** (zero slope at mid-span).

A worked illustration of the economy: for a cantilever with a point load W at the free end, the M/EI diagram is a triangle of height WL/EI and base L. Its area is **WL²/2EI** — the slope at the free end — and its centroid is at 2L/3 from the fixed end, so the moment of the area is (WL²/2EI)(2L/3) = **WL³/3EI**, the deflection. Two lines, no integration.

They are also the natural tool for a beam of **varying EI** (a haunched or stepped beam), because the M/EI diagram simply changes shape where EI changes, whereas Macaulay's method would need a separate equation for each segment.

**The conjugate beam method** restates the same idea as an analogy. Load an imaginary "conjugate" beam with the **M/EI diagram** as its loading; then

| On the conjugate beam | Gives on the real beam |
|---|---|
| **Shear force** | **Slope** |
| **Bending moment** | **Deflection** |

The supports must be transformed too, so that the conjugate beam's shear and moment reproduce the real beam's slope and deflection conditions:

| Real beam | Conjugate beam |
|---|---|
| **Simple support** (y = 0, θ ≠ 0) | **Simple support** |
| **Fixed end** (y = 0, θ = 0) | **Free end** |
| **Free end** (y ≠ 0, θ ≠ 0) | **Fixed end** |
| Interior support of a continuous beam | Internal hinge |
| Internal hinge | Interior support |

Notice that **fixed and free exchange places** — which is the whole trick, and the source of most errors in using the method. Its appeal is that once the conjugate beam is set up, the work is ordinary statics: find reactions, shear and moment, and read off slope and deflection.

**Which method to choose:**

| Method | Best for |
|---|---|
| **Macaulay** | Several point loads; a general expression for y(x) is wanted |
| **Moment-area** | Cantilevers; symmetrical loading; **varying EI** |
| **Conjugate beam** | The same cases as moment-area, if statics is preferred to geometry |
| **Unit load / Castigliano** | **Trusses**; frames; a deflection at **one specific point** |

sections.heading: Energy methods
sections.body:
**Strain energy** stored in a member:

| Mode | Strain energy |
|---|---|
| **Axial** | **P²L/(2AE)** |
| **Bending** | **∫ M² dx/(2EI)** |
| Torsion | T²L/(2GJ) |
| Shear | ∫ V² dx/(2AG) — usually negligible |

**Castigliano's first theorem** (the one used for deflections):

> **δ = ∂U/∂P**

The deflection at the point of application of a load, in the direction of that load, equals the **partial derivative of the total strain energy with respect to that load**. If no load acts where the deflection is wanted, apply a **dummy load Q**, differentiate, then set Q = 0.

Differentiating under the integral gives the practical forms:

> **Trusses: δ = Σ (P k L)/(A E)**
> **Beams and frames: δ = ∫ (M m dx)/(E I)**

where **P and M** are the forces due to the **actual loads** and **k and m** those due to a **unit load** applied at the point and in the direction of the required deflection. This is the **unit load method**, and it is the most generally useful hand technique in structural analysis, because it computes a deflection **anywhere, in any direction, including rotation** (apply a unit **couple** instead of a unit force).

For a **truss** the method is entirely arithmetic: tabulate each member's length, area, actual force P and unit-load force k, form PkL/AE for each, and sum. It also handles **temperature change** (δ = Σ k α ΔT L) and **fabrication error** (δ = Σ k ΔL) with no extra theory — which is why it is preferred over energy differentiation in practice.

**Maxwell's reciprocal theorem:**

> The deflection at **A** due to a unit load at **B** equals the deflection at **B** due to a unit load at **A**.

Generalised by **Betti's law** to any two load systems. Its consequences are more useful than the statement:

- The **flexibility and stiffness matrices are SYMMETRIC**, which halves the computation in matrix analysis and provides a check on any assembled matrix.
- It is the theoretical basis of **influence lines**, via the **Müller-Breslau principle**.

**Müller-Breslau principle:**

> The **influence line for any function** (reaction, shear, moment) has the **same shape as the deflected structure** when the corresponding restraint is **released and a unit displacement applied**.

So the influence line for a **reaction** is obtained by removing the support and displacing it by unity; for a **bending moment** at a section, by inserting a **hinge** there and applying a unit relative rotation; for **shear**, by inserting a shear release and applying a unit relative displacement. For determinate structures this gives straight-line influence diagrams immediately, without any analysis — which is why the principle is worth knowing even though it looks abstract.

**Castigliano's second theorem** (∂U/∂δ = P) and the **theorem of least work** are used for **indeterminate** structures, where the redundant forces take the values that **minimise the strain energy**. That is the energy route to the same answers the force method gives.

sections.heading: Influence lines and moving loads
sections.body:
An **influence line** shows how a function **at ONE FIXED SECTION** varies as a **unit load moves** across the structure.

**It must not be confused with a bending moment diagram**, which shows the function **along the structure for a FIXED load**. The distinction is worth stating in both directions:

| Diagram | Varies along | For |
|---|---|---|
| **Bending moment diagram** | **Position on the beam** | A **fixed** load system |
| **Influence line** | **Position of the unit load** | A **fixed** section |

**Standard influence lines for a simply supported beam of span L:**

| Function at section distance a from the left (b from the right) | Influence line |
|---|---|
| **Reaction R_A** | A straight line from **1 at A** to **0 at B** |
| **Bending moment at the section** | A **triangle** with peak **ab/L** at the section |
| **Shear at the section** | **Two parallel lines**, with a **step of 1** at the section: −a/L rising to +b/L |

The **peak of the moment influence line, ab/L**, is worth memorising: it is maximised when a = b = L/2, giving **L/4** — consistent with the standard WL/4 result.

**How influence lines are used.** For a load system, the effect is

> **Effect = Σ (P_i × ordinate under P_i)** for point loads
> **Effect = w × (area of the influence line under the load)** for a UDL

So a UDL should cover the whole of the **positive** region of the influence line to maximise a positive effect — which is why, for the shear at a section, the UDL is placed on **one side only**, and why in a continuous beam the pattern of loaded and unloaded spans matters. That last point is the practical origin of **pattern loading** requirements in codes.

**Moving loads on a simply supported beam** — the standard results:

| Quantity | Maximum when |
|---|---|
| **Maximum reaction** | The heaviest load is **at the support** |
| **Absolute maximum shear** | The load system is at a support |
| **Maximum moment at a GIVEN section** | One wheel is **at that section** |
| **Absolute maximum bending moment** | Found by trial — occurs when the load system is placed so that its **resultant is close to mid-span** |

The **absolute maximum moment** is an optimisation, not a formula: for a single point load it occurs at mid-span; for two or more loads the position must be found by trial, and a useful guide is that the section where it occurs bisects the distance between the resultant of the loads on the beam and the nearer support.

For a **single point load W** crossing a span: maximum moment **WL/4** at mid-span, maximum shear **W** at either support.

For a **UDL shorter than the span**: the maximum moment at a section occurs when the load is positioned so the section **divides the load in the same ratio as it divides the span**.

**Equivalent uniformly distributed load (EUDL)** is the device used in bridge codes: the actual train or vehicle loading is replaced by a UDL producing the **same maximum moment**, tabulated against span. It simplifies design at the cost of some accuracy, and is why IRC and railway bridge codes give EUDL tables rather than requiring a full moving-load analysis.

**Impact factor.** A moving load produces greater effects than the same load applied statically, because of the vertical acceleration of the vehicle over surface irregularities. Codes therefore add an **impact allowance**:

> **IRC Class A and B loading: impact factor = 4.5/(6 + L)** for concrete bridges, with L in metres

decreasing with span, because a long span responds more slowly than a short one and the impulse is spread over more of the structure.

**Where this material is applied:** **bridge girders**, **crane gantry girders** (where the moving load is the crane wheels), **industrial floors carrying trucks**, and the assessment of an existing bridge for a heavier vehicle — the last being a common professional task, and one where an influence line is exactly the right tool.

formulas.label: The elastic curve
formulas.expression: EI d²y/dx² = M ;   Macaulay: ⟨x − a⟩ⁿ = 0 when x ≤ a
formulas.note: Never expand a negative bracket. Extend a partial UDL to the end and cancel it with an upward one.

formulas.label: Standard maximum deflections
formulas.expression: SS point load WL³/48EI ;  SS UDL 5wL⁴/384EI ;  cantilever point WL³/3EI ;  cantilever UDL wL⁴/8EI
formulas.note: Fixed beam under UDL: wL⁴/384EI, one fifth of the simply supported value.

formulas.label: Span dominance
formulas.note: Doubling the span multiplies deflection 8- or 16-fold, but moment only 2- or 4-fold.

formulas.label: IS 456 span/depth limits
formulas.expression: cantilever 7 ;  simply supported 20 ;  continuous 26   (× 10/span beyond 10 m)
formulas.note: Deemed-to-satisfy. Final deflection limited to span/250; post-partition deflection to span/350 or 20 mm.

formulas.label: Mohr's theorems (moment-area)
formulas.expression: Δθ = area of the M/EI diagram ;   δ = moment of that area about the point
formulas.note: Best for cantilevers, symmetric loading and VARYING EI.

formulas.label: Conjugate beam analogy
formulas.expression: Load the conjugate beam with M/EI: its shear = real slope, its moment = real deflection
formulas.note: Fixed and free supports EXCHANGE places in the transformation.

formulas.label: Unit load method
formulas.expression: trusses δ = Σ PkL/(AE) ;   beams δ = ∫ Mm dx/(EI)
formulas.note: P, M from actual loads; k, m from a unit load at the point. A unit COUPLE gives rotation.

formulas.label: Castigliano's first theorem
formulas.expression: δ = ∂U/∂P     (apply a dummy load Q where no load acts, then set Q = 0)
formulas.note: U = P²L/2AE axial, ∫M²dx/2EI bending, T²L/2GJ torsion.

formulas.label: Influence line for a simply supported beam
formulas.expression: Moment at a: triangle of peak ab/L.   Shear at a: two parallel lines with a step of 1.
formulas.note: Effect = Σ(P × ordinate), or w × (area under the load) for a UDL.

formulas.label: Impact factor (IRC, concrete bridges)
formulas.note: Decreases with span, because a long span responds more slowly to the impulse.
